title: A Alibi for the Parish Again
premise: When matriarch Edwina Voss is buried, estate lawyer Kestrel Crane reads a will dated three days after her death—an impossible document that disinherits her entire family in favor of an heir no one can find. A confession letter arrives postmarked the day after the funeral, unsigned, claiming Edwina was poisoned and that Kestrel himself once filed away the evidence. As Kestrel investigates his own archive of twelve years of parish secrets, he discovers the killer is someone who has read every file he's ever kept—someone who has been using his own meticulous records to erase a second identity, a second life, and a first murder. The trail ends at the parish itself, where Kestrel must expose the killer during the reading of the fraudulent will, nearly becoming the final entry in someone else's file before turning the archive against its author.
about_author: Ivo Delacroix is the pseudonym of a former small-town archivist who spent a decade cataloguing probate records and the silences between them. Their mysteries are known for paper trails, buried identities, and villains who weaponize bureaucracy.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel Crane. At Edwina Voss's funeral, Kestrel is handed a will dated three days after her death—legally impossible. He reads it aloud under pressure from the family, disinheriting everyone for a mysterious 'M. Ashcombe.' The emotional beat is dread: his ordered world has produced a document that cannot exist.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. A confession letter arrives claiming Edwina was poisoned, postmarked the day after her funeral, and referencing a file Kestrel sealed twelve years ago. He burns nothing and tells no one, but begins quietly pulling his own archive. Beat: guilty recognition that his tidiness may have buried a crime.

chapters.title: The Crane Method
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Flashback-tinged chapter establishing his system: twelve years of parish secrets alphabetized in the vestry archive. He checks the 2013 file—Halloway's drowning—and finds pages re-ordered, a page missing. Beat: cold fear; someone has been inside his files.

chapters.title: The Disinherited
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. He interviews the furious Voss heirs—son Aldous, daughter-in-law Petra, granddaughter Wren—who each claim Edwina promised them everything. Wren, the black-sheep archivist, notices Kestrel's unease and starts asking her own questions. Beat: suspicion turned outward, alliances forming.

chapters.title: M. Ashcombe
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. The named heir doesn't exist in any registry, but the initials match a 2013 baptism record Kestrel himself filed. He realizes the will's forger used parish records—his records. Beat: the hunt turns inward; he is evidence.

chapters.title: A Second Funeral
chapters.summary: POV Wren Voss. Wren's chapter: she finds her grandmother's hidden diary referencing 'the boy in the water' and 'the lawyer who keeps everything.' She confronts Kestrel; he deflects, but she sees the sealed 2013 box. Beat: two investigators circling the same wound, neither trusting the other.

chapters.title: The Vestry at Night
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Kestrel stakes out the archive and catches a figure—too dark to identify—who leaves a second letter: a page from Halloway's file and a threat: 'Stop reading, Kestrel.' Beat: escalation; the killer is watching him read.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Silence
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. He reconstructs the Halloway drowning: ruled accidental, closed in nine days, and he was the junior lawyer who notarized the paperwork without question. His mentor, Canon Pell, signed the death certificate. Beat: shame; his loyalty to the parish curdled into complicity.

chapters.title: Petra's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Petra Voss is caught shredding financial records—Edwina had discovered the family business was insolvent. Petra becomes the obvious suspect, too obvious. Kestrel notes her alibi is airtight because someone gave it to her. Beat: the frame within the frame.

chapters.title: The Canon's Hands
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Kestrel confronts the aging Canon Pell, who admits Edwina summoned him the night she died—she'd found the truth about Halloway and meant to expose it. Pell swears he left her alive. Beat: grief and dread; the truth was already loose before the funeral.

chapters.title: Alphabet of the Dead
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren decodes her grandmother's diary cipher and finds a name half-erased: not Halloway's killer, but Halloway's true identity—he was living in the parish under another name. Beat: revelation that the drowning victim was himself a fiction.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Halloway
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Kestrel traces Halloway's alias to a second life, a hidden family—and realizes M. Ashcombe is that family's descendant, the true heir Edwina meant to restore. The will is fraudulent, but its beneficiary may be legitimate. Beat: moral vertigo; the forgery aims at justice.

chapters.title: Missing Pages
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. The archive is broken into; the entire 2013 box is gone, and Kestrel's own personnel file is disturbed—someone has been studying him for years. Beat: paranoia; the killer knows his habits, his handwriting, his silences.

chapters.title: What Petra Knew
chapters.summary: POV Petra. Petra's chapter: terrified, she admits Edwina blackmailed the family for years over the drowning—Edwina witnessed it and stayed silent for money. Petra's alibi came from a phone call she can't account for. Beat: the family's inheritance was built on a buried body.

chapters.title: The Call
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Kestrel replays the phone records: the call giving Petra her alibi came from the vestry. Only three people have archive keys—him, Pell, and the verger, Silas Morden, the quiet man who has served the parish for twenty years. Beat: the trap narrows.

chapters.title: Silas Morden, In His Own Words
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Kestrel pulls Silas's employment file and finds the same alias pattern as Halloway—Silas arrived in the parish the year after the drowning, under a name Kestrel himself verified. Beat: horrified understanding; he built the killer's identity with his own hands.

chapters.title: Confession, Unsigned
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. A third letter arrives: a full confession in Kestrel's own handwriting style, dated and notarized—forged so Kestrel will hang for Edwina's murder. The killer intends to close the file on him. Beat: checkmate approaching; time is nearly out.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Kestrel requests a formal second reading of the will to authenticate it, knowing the forger must attend to protect the Ashcombe claim. The vestry fills with heirs, Pell, and Silas. Beat: coiled tension; the trap is set with himself as bait.

chapters.title: Every File Has an Author
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Climax. Kestrel reveals the will's paper stock came from the vestry supply and reads aloud the archive's access log—Silas's key, every missing night. Silas, cornered, confesses: he is Halloway's brother, who came for truth and stayed for revenge, killing Edwina when she tried to confess. He draws the knife meant for Kestrel. Beat: violence erupting among the shelves.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Wren intervenes; Silas is subdued, wounded, and taken. In the aftermath, Pell collapses—his twelve-year-old signature on the false drowning report. Kestrel chooses truth over the parish's peace: he hands the reopened file to the police, including his own complicity. Beat: costly integrity.

chapters.title: Probate
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. The real will surfaces in Edwina's diary's cipher, leaving everything to M. Ashcombe's family with a letter of apology. Kestrel executes it faithfully, disinheriting the Vosses and restoring the drowned man's name. Beat: bittersweet justice; the archive finally tells the truth.

chapters.title: Alphabetized, At Last
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Months later, Kestrel resigns from the parish, donates the archive to the county with every secret unsealed, and visits Silas in prison—two keepers of files, one redeemed by honesty, one by exposure. He keeps a single blank folder, unlabeled. Beat: quiet renewal; identity no longer hidden, but chosen.
